parts.rubric: 1 point for a valid, specific solution (e.g., issuing fish consumption advisories limiting how often/which species people eat, dredging and removing contaminated sediment, requiring stricter discharge limits and monitoring at the industrial facility going forward). 1 point for a realistic tradeoff (e.g., consumption advisories reduce food security or cultural fishing practices for local/subsistence or Indigenous communities; sediment dredging is extremely costly and can temporarily re-suspend contaminants; stricter regulations may raise costs for the facility and regional employment).

title: Dose-Response Relationships and Pesticide Risk Assessment

stimulus.title: Dose-Response Curve for Pesticide X in a Laboratory Test Population

prompt: Toxicologists exposed a test population of laboratory animals to varying doses of Pesticide X and recorded the percent mortality at each dose, shown in the graph. Regulators are using this dose-response data to help set a legal exposure limit for agricultural workers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using the graph, identify the approximate LD50 for Pesticide X and explain what this value represents.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly identifying the LD50 as approximately 10 mg/kg body weight (the dose at which the curve crosses 50% mortality). 1 point for correctly explaining that LD50 is the dose of a substance lethal to 50% of the test population within a specified exposure period.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe the general shape of the curve shown in the graph and explain what this shape indicates about the relationship between dose and toxicity for most substances.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly describing the curve as sigmoidal/S-shaped, with mortality increasing slowly at low doses, rising sharply through the middle dose range, then leveling off at high doses. 1 point for explaining that this shape reflects individual variation in sensitivity within a population — some individuals are affected at low doses while others are more resistant, so response accumulates gradually rather than as an abrupt on/off effect.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A farmworker is regularly exposed to low doses of Pesticide X that would each individually cause less than 5% mortality risk in this dataset. Explain why regulators might still be concerned about this worker's long-term health, referencing the concept of chronic toxicity.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly distinguishing this scenario from the acute, single-dose toxicity shown in the graph. 1 point for explaining that chronic toxicity results from repeated, long-term exposure to lower doses, which can cause cumulative damage, bioaccumulation of the substance in tissue, or other sub-lethal health effects (e.g., endocrine disruption, cancer risk, organ damage) that are not captured by a single acute LD50 dose-response curve.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Propose one specific policy that regulators could implement to protect agricultural workers from long-term Pesticide X exposure, and explain how it directly reduces exposure risk.
parts.rubric: 1 point for a specific, valid policy (e.g., mandatory personal protective equipment requirements, restricted-entry intervals after application, maximum allowable residue limits, mandatory rotation to reduce exposure frequency, or a required buffer zone between application sites and worker areas). 1 point for a clear mechanistic explanation of how the policy reduces the dose or frequency of exposure the worker receives. 1 point for connecting the reduced exposure back to the dose-response relationship — i.e., lowering the effective dose received moves workers further left on the curve, reducing both acute and cumulative chronic risk.

title: Stratospheric Ozone Recovery and the Montreal Protocol

stimulus.title: Antarctic Ozone Hole Maximum Area, 1980-2020
stimulus.sourceNote: Approximate values based on NASA/NOAA satellite ozone monitoring records

prompt: The graph shows the maximum area of the Antarctic ozone hole from 1980 to 2020. The Montreal Protocol, an international treaty phasing out the production of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting substances, was signed in 1987 and has been amended and strengthened several times since.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the overall trend in ozone hole area shown in the graph from 1980 to 2006, and the trend from 2006 to 2020.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly describing the increasing trend from 1980 (2 million km²) to a peak around 2006 (29 million km²). 1 point for correctly describing the leveling off/gradual decline from 2006 to 2020 (from 29 to about 20 million km²).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the chemical mechanism by which CFCs released at Earth's surface lead to the destruction of stratospheric ozone.
parts.rubric: 1 point for explaining that CFCs are stable/persistent in the lower atmosphere and are transported to the stratosphere over time. 1 point for explaining that ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere breaks apart CFC molecules, releasing free chlorine atoms. 1 point for explaining that each chlorine atom acts as a catalyst, breaking apart thousands of ozone (O3) molecules into O2 without being consumed itself, allowing continued ozone destruction from a single chlorine atom over a long period.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Using the graph, explain why the ozone hole did not immediately shrink after the Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987, even though it continued to grow for nearly two more decades.
parts.rubric: 1 point for noting the long time lag between signing/phase-out and recovery evident in the graph (continued growth through 2006). 1 point for a valid mechanistic explanation: CFCs already released before the phase-out have very long atmospheric lifetimes (50-100+ years) and continued to reach and react in the stratosphere for decades, so existing chlorine reservoirs kept depleting ozone even after new production was reduced/banned.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe one specific consequence to human health OR ecosystems that results from increased UV radiation reaching Earth's surface due to ozone depletion, and explain the mechanism of harm.
parts.rubric: 1 point for identifying a valid consequence (e.g., increased skin cancer incidence, increased cataract rates in humans, or reduced phytoplankton productivity/DNA damage in aquatic organisms). 1 point for a correct mechanism (e.g., UV radiation directly damages DNA in skin cells causing mutations that can lead to cancer; UV damages proteins in the eye lens causing cataracts; UV penetrates surface ocean water and damages phytoplankton DNA, reducing primary productivity at the base of marine food webs).

title: Ocean Acidification, Coral Calcification, and Reef Ecosystem Impacts

stimulus.title: Coral Calcification Rate vs. Seawater pH
stimulus.sourceNote: Hypothetical data for this exercise, illustrating a pattern consistent with published ocean acidification research

prompt: Ocean surface pH has declined from a pre-industrial average of approximately 8.2 as the ocean has absorbed increasing amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide. Researchers exposed coral samples to seawater at different pH levels and measured their calcification (skeleton-building) rate relative to the pre-industrial baseline, shown in the scatter plot.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between seawater pH and coral calcification rate shown in the scatter plot.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly describing a positive relationship: as pH decreases (more acidic), calcification rate decreases. 1 point for citing supporting data (e.g., calcification drops from 100% at pH 8.2 to about 38% at pH 7.8) or correctly describing the trend as roughly linear over this range.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the chemical mechanism by which increasing atmospheric CO2 concentrations lower ocean pH.
parts.rubric: 1 point for explaining that atmospheric CO2 dissolves into seawater. 1 point for explaining that dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates and releases hydrogen ions (H+), lowering the pH of the water.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why lower pH specifically reduces the ability of corals (and other calcifying organisms) to build calcium carbonate skeletons or shells.
parts.rubric: 1 point for explaining that the excess hydrogen ions react with carbonate ions (CO3²⁻) in seawater, converting them to bicarbonate (HCO3-) and reducing the concentration of carbonate ions available. 1 point for explaining that calcifying organisms require sufficient carbonate ion concentration to combine with calcium and precipitate calcium carbonate (CaCO3) for their skeletons/shells, so reduced carbonate availability directly slows or impairs this process.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Identify one ecosystem service provided by coral reefs that would be lost or degraded if reef-building slows significantly due to ocean acidification, and explain the connection between reduced calcification and the loss of that service.
parts.rubric: 1 point for identifying a valid ecosystem service (e.g., coastal storm/wave protection, fisheries habitat and biodiversity support, or tourism/recreation revenue). 1 point for a clear explanation linking reduced calcification to the loss of that service — e.g., slower reef growth and increased structural erosion reduce the physical reef structure that dissipates wave energy and protects coastlines, or reduces the complex habitat structure that supports high fish biodiversity and fisheries productivity.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Ocean acidification and ocean warming often occur simultaneously and both stress coral reefs. Explain why addressing only local stressors (such as reducing nutrient runoff or overfishing near a reef) would be insufficient to fully protect coral reefs from these two global stressors.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly noting that ocean acidification and warming are driven by global atmospheric CO2 concentrations, not local conditions, so local management cannot reduce their severity. 1 point for explaining that meaningfully addressing these stressors requires global reductions in greenhouse gas/CO2 emissions, meaning local conservation efforts, while valuable for other stressors (like nutrient pollution or overfishing), cannot on their own prevent acidification- or warming-driven coral decline.

title: Habitat Fragmentation, Invasive Species, and Biodiversity Loss in a National Park

stimulus.title: Bird Species Richness and Presence of Invasive Predators in Forest Patches

prompt: Ecologists surveyed four forest patches within and around a national park that vary in size, connectivity to other patches via wildlife corridors, and the presence of an invasive predator (a nonnative mammal that preys on ground-nesting birds). Bird species richness was recorded for each patch.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Using the data in the table, compare bird species richness between Patch A and Patch B, and propose a hypothesis for why they differ, based only on the variables shown.
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly noting that Patch A has higher bird species richness (34) than Patch B (24). 1 point for a hypothesis correctly attributing the difference to patch size and/or connectivity (Patch A is much larger and connected, while Patch B is small and isolated), since neither has the invasive predator, isolating these as the likely explanatory variables.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the ecological mechanism by which habitat fragmentation (small, isolated patches) reduces species richness, independent of the effects of invasive species.
parts.rubric: 1 point for explaining that smaller patches support smaller populations, which are more vulnerable to local extinction from random events (demographic/environmental stochasticity). 1 point for explaining that isolation limits dispersal and gene flow between patches, increasing inbreeding and reducing genetic diversity, further increasing extinction risk. 1 point for explaining that fragmentation increases the ratio of edge habitat to interior habitat, which favors generalist/edge-adapted species over interior-dependent specialist species, altering community composition and often reducing richness of sensitive species.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Using the data in the table, describe the effect of the invasive predator on bird species richness by comparing patches of similar size and connectivity (Patch A vs. Patch C, and Patch B vs. Patch D).
parts.rubric: 1 point for correctly noting that among large, connected patches, richness is lower with the invasive predator present (Patch C: 26) than without it (Patch A: 34). 1 point for correctly noting the same pattern among small, isolated patches (Patch D: 13, with predator, versus Patch B: 24, without), supporting the conclusion that the invasive predator independently reduces richness regardless of patch size/connectivity.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Propose one specific conservation strategy to improve bird species richness in Patch D, and explain how it addresses one of the two stressors identified in this study (fragmentation or invasive predation).
parts.rubric: 1 point for a specific, valid strategy (e.g., establishing a wildlife corridor connecting Patch D to a larger patch, or implementing an invasive predator removal/control program in Patch D). 1 point for a clear explanation connecting the strategy to the relevant mechanism — e.g., a corridor would increase effective patch size and allow gene flow/recolonization, directly addressing the fragmentation stressor; predator removal would directly reduce nest predation pressure on ground-nesting birds, addressing the invasive species stressor.
